catalog_quote: Urdu stress is sensitive to syllable weight. This weight can be represented by moraic count of each syllable [7]. ... long vowels are bi-moriac and short vowels are mono-moraic in Urdu. In addition, each coda consonant has a weight equivalent to a single mora [4], [9]. ... Syllables can be mono-moraic (light), bi-moraic (heavy) and tri-moraic (super-heavy, e.g. closed syllables with long vowels). ... Analysis shows that heavy and super-heavy syllables may take primary or secondary stress. Primary stress is assigned to the first bi-moraic or tri-moraic syllables from the end of the word. Light syllables do not take stress. However, final syllables do not take stress even if they are heavy, indicating that the final mora is extrametrical [4]. sweep_summary: Three title hits, all already in the per-language bibliography. (1) Butt/Jabeen/Bögel 2016 (Linguistic Analysis 40) is sentence-level wh-phrase prosody, not word stress; paywalled (journal sells the article, no DOI, KOPS record metadata-only, ResearchGate 403); low priority. (2) Hussain 1997 Northwestern dissertation, which earlier passes recorded as 'not online', IS online at the CLE URL that Glottolog itself lists (https://www.cle.org.pk/Publication/theses/1997/); fetched sources (5.95 MB UMI scan, no text layer), scanned the front matter and the stress chapter (diss. pp. 39-52) one page at a time, and read the rule first-hand: final mora extrametrical, rightmost heavy syllable stressed, final syllable only if super-heavy, penult if all light, one stress per word, 'fixed stress... weakly variable'. (3) Hussain 2007 is the UMI reprint of the same dissertation (Glottolog note), so a duplicate. The 1997 statement confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and refines it by dropping the hedge; the current deciding source (Hussain 2005) is the author's later revision adding secondary stresses. Semantic Scholar returned 429.

new_statements.quote: Generalizing over all words, if a final syllable belongs to {super-heavy} it is stressed, and if it belongs to {light, heavy} it is not stressed. If a final syllable is not super-heavy, the syllable belonging to {heavy, super-heavy} closest to the end of the word is stressed. And if the final syllable is not super-heavy and there are no syllables belonging to {heavy, super-heavy} preceding the final syllable, the penultimate syllable is stressed. [p. 50:] The whole stress algorithm can then be simplified into the statement that the last heavy syllable is stressed (syllable weights counted after subtracting away the extrametricality effect in the final syllable). If all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Hussain, Sarmad. 1997. Phonetic Correlates of Lexical Stress in Urdu. PhD dissertation, Northwestern University (UMI 9814230).
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2, 'The Urdu language' > 'Lexical stress', diss. pp. 48-49 (PDF pp. 64-65); simplified restatement p. 50 (PDF p. 66)
new_statements.reading: Text is scanned of a UMI scan (one '}' and 'last' were scanned-garbled and are restored here; everything else verbatim). Urdu word stress is quantity-sensitive and unbounded, assigned right-to-left: with the final mora extrametrical, the rightmost heavy (multi-moraic) syllable is stressed; a final syllable takes stress only when super-heavy (VVC/VCC); if no syllable is heavy, default is the penult. One stress per word (p. 51); author calls it 'a fixed stress language' with 'signs of being a weakly variable stress language' (a few grammatically related minimal pairs, p. 50). Evidence base: dictionary stress marks (Qureshi 1992) over all licensed 2-3 syllable weight templates. This is consistent with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and removes the hedge: the multiple-stress / speaker-variation caveats come only from the author's later 2005 conference paper (the current deciding source), which keeps the same primary-stress rule but adds secondary stresses per morpheme from informal Lahore speaker feedback (Jabeen 2019 diss. pp. 44-45 criticizes that addition). Recommend citing the 1997 dissertation as the primary statement (rightmost heavy with final-mora extrametricality, else penult) and keeping Hussain 2005 as a note on secondary stress and variation.

sources.quote: p. 50 (scanned): "If the extrametricality is taken into account, the super-heavy/heavy distinction becomes a heavy/light distinction in final syllable. The whole stress algorithm can then be simplified into the statement that the last heavy syllable is stressed (syllable weights counted after subtracting away the extrametricality effect in the final syllable). If all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed. The same stress assignment algorithm can be extended for words with more than three syllables. These results show that Urdu is a fixed stress language. Yet Urdu also shows signs of being a weakly variable stress language."
sources.locator: Ch. 2, section 'The Urdu language' > 'Lexical stress', diss. pp. 45-51 (= PDF pp. 61-67); rule stated pp. 48-50; extrametricality argument p. 49; 'fixed stress... weakly variable' and minimal pair p. 50; single stress per word p. 51
sources.note: Weight-based, right-to-left, unbounded: short V = 1 mora, long V = 2, each coda C = 1 (p. 44); the final mora of the word is extrametrical (p. 49), so a final syllable is stressed only if super-heavy (VVC/VCC); otherwise the rightmost heavy/super-heavy syllable is stressed; if none, the penult (pp. 48-49). Evidence: stress marks in Qureshi 1992 Standard Twentieth Century Dictionary for all licensed 2- and 3-syllable weight combinations (table (2.11), pp. 47-48). sources.quote: 'Stress in Urdu depends on syllable weight, and has been explored by Hussain (2004), who proposed an Urdu phonological stress-marking algorithm. This algorithm classifies Urdu syllables as either monomoraic, bimoraic, or trimoraic. Given these definitions, the algorithm states that a trimoraic (i.e., super-heavy) syllable in final position is stressed; if the final syllable is not trimoraic, then the rightmost non-final bimoraic (i.e., heavy) or trimoraic (i.e., super-heavy) syllable is stressed; and if all syllables are monomoraic (i.e., light), the penultimate syllable is stressed. sources.quote: 'As far as phonological analysis of stress in Urdu is concerned, it depends on the weight of the syllable and is explored by Hussain [1] ... starting from the end of the word, the first heavy syllable is always stressed in Urdu, and if all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed.' The phonological algorithm matches expert perceptual stress marking on 70% of syllables (544-word set), supporting the HEDGED firmness.
sources.note: Quantifies the fit of the phonological rule against expert perceptual marking (70%), a second number beside Nyyar's ~80% for the exceptions/firmness fields.

Given these definitions, Hussain (1997) explains that the last heavy syllable is stressed, and if all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed.
